data.synopsis#Synopsis:
circleci-migrate helps you move data — contexts, project settings, environment variables, and more — from one CircleCI organisation to another.
Typical workflow:
Export the source organisation to a local manifest file: circleci-migrate export --source-token $SRC_TOKEN --source-org gh/myorg
(Optional) Review or edit the manifest.
Sync the manifest into the destination organisation (the destination org is inferred from the manifest; no --source-org flag is needed): circleci-migrate sync --dest-token $DST_TOKEN --manifest manifest.json --apply
Or run both steps in one shot: circleci-migrate migrate --source-token $SRC_TOKEN --dest-token $DST_TOKEN --source-org gh/myorg --dest-org gh/neworg
Use "circleci-migrate [command] --help" for more information about a command.

data.synopsis#Synopsis:
cutover performs the final switch of a migration: it stops builds in the SOURCE org and turns builds on in the DESTINATION org, recording every change so it can be reversed. It is a DRY RUN unless --apply is given.
--pause-source For each source project, pause it reversibly: set the v1.1 feature flag drop-all-build-requests=true on OAuth/VCS projects (the prior value is recorded), and disable the source triggers that are enabled and are not github_oauth triggers (the ids are recorded). github_oauth triggers cannot be disabled through the API, so OAuth projects rely on the flag. Projects are NEVER unfollowed (that is destructive). --pause-org Also set drop-all-build-requests=true on the whole source org (the org-level flag overrides every project). Use with --pause-source. --enable-dest Enable the destination triggers whose source counterpart was enabled. A destination trigger is matched to its source trigger by name first, then by its defining fields; when several destination triggers match equally well and the source triggers differ in enabled/disabled state, the item is reported "manual" and nothing is enabled. A trigger that was disabled in the source stays disabled, and a project the manifest shows as paused (drop_all_build_requests=true) or not followed is skipped ("manual"). Run sync --apply first so the destination triggers exist. With --pause-source or --pause-org in the same run, a failed pause step stops the run before anything is enabled (non-zero exit). --undo Restore everything recorded in the state file: source flags back to their prior values, the source triggers it disabled re-enabled, and the destination triggers it enabled disabled again. Needs only --state (and --apply to act); it fails if the state file does not exist. A client (and token) is needed only for the side(s) that have records. Pass --manifest (and --mapping) as well to have the state's source/destination org checked against them.
Every change is written to the state file (--state, default cutover-state.json, mode 0600) BEFORE it is made, so --undo works even after a partial failure. Re-running is idempotent: items already in the wanted state report "exists". Each item is printed with its outcome and the command exits non-zero if any item failed.
Order for a clean cutover (docs/migrations/oauth-to-app.md has the full sequence): freeze merges; sync --skip-pipelines --apply; secrets transfer ... --apply (it must run BEFORE the source is paused); cutover --pause-source --apply; uninstall the GitHub App from the source and install it on the destination; sync --apply --webhook-secrets-out ; cutover --enable-dest --apply; validate. If something is wrong, cutover --undo --apply returns the source to its previous state. Keep the state file (it lets --undo work) and the webhook secrets file (it holds secrets) safe until the cutover is confirmed.
CAUTION: once the GitHub App is UNINSTALLED from the source GitHub org, the source's GitHub App triggers no longer exist, so they can neither be disabled nor re-enabled; pausing then relies on drop-all-build-requests alone, and --undo can only restore that flag. Pause the source BEFORE uninstalling the App.
Source actions use the source token (--source-token / CIRCLECI_SOURCE_TOKEN, else --token); destination actions use the destination token (--dest-token / CIRCLECI_DEST_TOKEN, else --token).
Examples: circleci-migrate cutover --manifest manifest.json --pause-source circleci-migrate cutover --manifest manifest.json --mapping mapping.json --pause-source --enable-dest --apply circleci-migrate cutover --manifest manifest.json --pause-source --pause-org --apply circleci-migrate cutover --undo --apply
circleci-migrate cutover [--pause-source] [--pause-org] [--enable-dest] [--undo] --manifest [--apply] [flags]

data.synopsis#Synopsis:
export reads configuration from the source CircleCI organization and writes a non-secret JSON manifest plus a human-readable audit report.
The manifest captures contexts (and their variable names, restrictions, and security groups), projects (settings, variable names, and metadata), and org-level settings. It is read-only: it never writes to CircleCI, and it never contains secret values — those are masked by the API and must be captured with the in-pipeline secrets step.
The org slug is "gh/" for GitHub OAuth organizations or "circleci/" for GitHub App / GitLab organizations.
Self-hosted runner resource classes live under a namespace on runner.circleci.com. Pass --runner-namespace to capture them. The namespace must be supplied explicitly because there is no clean org→namespace lookup in the CircleCI API.
USAGE DATA SNAPSHOT (opt-in):
Pass --include-usage to also request a historical usage report from the CircleCI Usage API. The report is downloaded as gzip-compressed CSV files to a "usage/" sub-directory next to the manifest. The window defaults to the last 30 days; use --usage-start / --usage-end (RFC 3339) to override. The maximum window is 31 days (enforced by the API).
IMPORTANT: usage data is a local baseline/record only. It does NOT transfer to the destination organisation during sync or migrate. If the usage export fails or times out, the main export succeeds and a warning is printed.
Examples: circleci-migrate export --source-org gh/acme --source-token $SRC_TOKEN circleci-migrate export --source-org gh/acme -o acme.json --report acme-audit.md circleci-migrate export --source-org gh/acme --project gh/acme/web --project gh/acme/api circleci-migrate export --source-org gh/acme --runner-namespace acme circleci-migrate export --source-org gh/acme --include-usage circleci-migrate export --source-org gh/acme --include-usage --usage-start 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z --usage-end 2026-01-31T23:59:59Z

data.synopsis#Synopsis:
generate lists the projects already onboarded in the destination org and matches them against the projects captured in the export manifest by repo name (the last '/'-separated segment of the slug, e.g. "web" from "gh/acme/web").
For VCS-integrated (GitHub / Bitbucket) destination orgs the dest slug is deterministic: //. When a source project has no onboarded dest project by that repo name, generate DERIVES the expected dest slug and writes it to mapping.json in a separate "derived" bucket. These entries let sync and secrets transfer proceed without manual mapping edits, but you must ensure the destination project is onboarded before running those commands (otherwise they will fail to find the project).
Only gh/ and bb/ providers support slug derivation. circleci/ (App/standalone) slugs contain UUIDs and cannot be derived — these projects remain "unmatched".
Output: • A mapping.json file ready for use with 'sync --mapping' and 'secrets transfer --mapping'. • A human-readable report printed to stdout with four sections: matched — source slug → dest slug (project onboarded, written) derived — source slug → derived dest slug (project NOT yet onboarded, written — create the project first, then re-run sync) unmatched — source projects with no derivable dest slug (circleci/ orgs) dest-only — dest projects with no source counterpart (info only)
Exit code is 0 even when there are unmatched entries — the report is the deliverable; unmatched entries mean the user must onboard those projects in the destination org first (or add manual entries to the mapping file).

data.synopsis#Synopsis:
migrate combines 'export' and 'sync' into a single command.
When run WITHOUT --source-org and --dest-org on an interactive terminal, migrate launches a guided walkthrough that prompts for each required value and lets you choose which parts of the org to migrate. This interactive mode is designed for first-time use and manual one-off migrations.
NOTE: interactive prompts are written to stderr; if you pipe stdout while relying on the guided prompts, use a TTY for stdin — piping stdin triggers non-TTY mode and skips all prompts (use --no-input to make this explicit).
When --source-org and --dest-org are provided, migrate runs non-interactively using only the supplied flags — suitable for scripting and CI pipelines. Pass --no-input (or run with stdin redirected / piped) to make the command error immediately if any required value is missing, instead of blocking on a prompt.
It reads data from the source CircleCI organisation (using the source token), builds an in-memory manifest, and immediately applies it to the destination organisation (using the dest token) — without requiring a manifest file on disk.
Secret VALUES are never exported via the API. If you have a captured secret bundle (produced by the in-pipeline 'secrets' step), pass it with --secrets. Without a bundle, all variable values are reported as needing manual entry (or use --missing-secrets=placeholder to write placeholder values).
IN-PIPELINE SECRETS TRANSFER (opt-in): Pass --transfer-secrets together with --dest-token-context to run the in-pipeline transfer step after sync completes. This transfers context env-var values directly from the source org to the destination org without writing any bundle to disk. Mutually exclusive with --secrets.
The project slug mapping is derived automatically from --source-org and --dest-org: for gh/ and bb/ dest orgs the dest slug is //; this is the same derivation used by 'mapping generate'. Pass --include-project-vars to also transfer project env-var values. Pass --include-ssh-keys to also transfer additional project SSH keys in-pipeline (zero-disk; private key material is never echoed to logs).
Requires: --dest-token-context source-org context that holds CIRCLECI_DEST_TOKEN --transfer-secrets opt-in flag to activate this step
See 'secrets transfer --help' for full documentation of the in-pipeline flow.
By default migrate performs a DRY RUN and writes nothing to the destination. Review the output, then re-run with --apply to write changes. Pass --yes / -y to auto-confirm enabling builds for newly-created projects without a prompt.
Use --output / -o to save the exported manifest to disk, and --report to save a human-readable audit document. Both flags are optional; omitting them keeps the migration entirely in-memory.
For more control — e.g. to inspect or edit the manifest between steps — run 'export' and 'sync' separately.

data.synopsis#Synopsis:
capture is the RECOMMENDED way to extract secret values from CircleCI.
It extracts plaintext environment-variable values WITHOUT committing any config to the target repository. The CLI builds an inline (unversioned) pipeline config, triggers a run inside CircleCI, and downloads the captured values automatically.
RECOMMENDED: run 'secrets capture' on an interactive terminal without flags to launch the guided walkthrough. It prompts for each option with sensible defaults and explicit guidance on host-project selection for context extraction.
NON-INTERACTIVE MODE & THE CAPTURE-ALL GUARD: Only --manifest is strictly required. Once --manifest is supplied (or stdin is not a TTY) capture runs non-interactively and does NOT launch the guided walkthrough. By default, when neither --context nor --project is given, capture would select EVERY context and project that has at least one env var in the manifest and trigger a REAL CircleCI extraction pipeline for each one.
To prevent accidental org-wide extraction (e.g. from a piped or recorded session), an unattended capture-all is FAIL-CLOSED: if the run is non-interactive, neither --context nor --project is set, and you have NOT passed --yes (or --no-input), capture errors out instead of triggering pipelines. You then have three options: 1. Pass --context and/or --project to scope exactly what is captured. 2. Pass --yes (or --no-input) to acknowledge an unattended capture-all. 3. Run on an interactive TTY (no --manifest) for the guided walkthrough.
Interactive prompts are written to stderr; if you pipe stdout while relying on the guided prompts, use a TTY for stdin — piping stdin triggers non-TTY mode.
For the orb-based alternative (committed config), see: circleci-migrate orb inline --help circleci-migrate secrets extract --help
HOW IT WORKS:
Reads variable names from the manifest for the selected project(s) and context(s). Checks the org-level allow_api_trigger_with_config flag BEFORE triggering any pipeline: If the flag is already ON → proceed normally. If it is OFF and --enable-trigger is set → enable it, defer restore. If it is OFF and running interactively → offer to enable (with auto-restore); answering "no" exits cleanly with guidance. If it is OFF and running non-interactively → fail fast with an actionable error before any pipeline is triggered (no mid-run failure). Ensures api-trigger-with-config is enabled for each project (either it must already be on, or --enable-trigger must be set). Triggers an unversioned pipeline run with an inline config that dumps the variable values to a build artifact. Polls until the pipeline completes, then downloads and parses the artifact. Writes the captured values into the secret bundle (--output). Restores the allow_api_trigger_with_config flag to its original value (even on failure). HOST PROJECT FOR CONTEXT EXTRACTION: Context env vars are injected into a job that references the context. The pipeline must run under some project — this is the "host project". Any project works; build history is irrelevant (only extraction matters). Use --host-project to specify it; the guided mode prompts you to choose. Project env vars are always captured under each project's own pipeline.
ENCRYPTION (default: ON — use --no-encrypt to opt out): By default, the in-pipeline extraction job encrypts the artifact with age so that plaintext secrets NEVER persist in CircleCI artifact storage. Encryption requires a public key: supply --ssh-public-key or --generate-key. When neither is given, capture auto-generates a fresh keypair (--generate-key behaviour).
After the run, capture downloads the .age artifact and decrypts it locally with --ssh-private-key (or the generated key) to build the in-memory bundle.
Use --no-encrypt to disable encryption and accept a PLAINTEXT artifact. This is strongly discouraged for production secrets — build artifacts are retained for at least 1 day and there is no delete-artifact API.
Use --generate-key to have capture create a fresh age X25519 keypair automatically, print the file paths, and use it for this run.
STORAGE (--storage): artifact (default) — store the bundle as a CircleCI job artifact. s3 — upload to S3 only (requires aws CLI + AWS creds in job). both — store in both artifact and S3.
For S3 storage provide --s3-bucket and (optionally) --s3-prefix. The job executor must have AWS credentials via a context or project env vars.
SECURITY NOTES:
Without --encrypt: the secret bundle contains plaintext secrets. Protect it. Build artifacts are retained for at least 1 day; there is no delete API. With --encrypt the artifact is age-encrypted so plaintext never hits disk. Rotate any captured secrets after migration. Examples:

data.synopsis#Synopsis:
transfer is a ZERO-DISK-WRITE mode for migrating context env-var VALUES directly from the SOURCE org to the DESTINATION org without producing any bundle file.
Instead of writing values to a build artifact (as 'secrets capture' does), 'secrets transfer' triggers a single dynamic pipeline in the SOURCE org with one job per context. Each job imports the source context (CircleCI unmasks the values into the job environment) and PUTs each value directly into the matching context in the DESTINATION org via the CircleCI API over TLS.
NO plaintext ever touches disk or build artifacts — strictly better security than the encrypted-bundle-artifact flow for context variables.
CREATE-MISSING DESTINATION CONTEXTS: When a destination context does not exist, the in-pipeline job creates it automatically (POST /api/v2/context) before setting env-var values. You no longer need to run 'sync --apply' first if you only want to fill values. The destination org must already exist; creating contexts within it is safe.
PROJECT ENV-VAR TRANSFER (opt-in with --include-project-vars): Pass --include-project-vars to also transfer project-level env-var values.
ADDITIONAL SSH KEY TRANSFER (opt-in with --include-ssh-keys): Pass --include-ssh-keys to transfer additional project SSH keys in-pipeline without writing private key material to disk or artifacts. The in-pipeline job uses add_ssh_keys to materialize each key, matches it by SHA256 fingerprint, reads the private key VERBATIM with jq --rawfile (never echoed), and POSTs it to the destination project via POST /api/v1.1/project/{slug}/ssh-key. A project with SSH keys but no env vars still triggers a per-project pipeline.
IMPORTANT: project env vars are strictly project-scoped — CircleCI only injects them when a pipeline runs under that exact project. Therefore, 'secrets transfer' triggers ONE SEPARATE PIPELINE per source project, each under that project's own slug. This is the only correct approach: a single shared host-project pipeline would silently produce blank values for every project that is not the host project (the bug this design explicitly prevents).
The destination project must already exist. Source project slug → destination project slug is resolved from an explicit --mapping entry (keys containing "/" in the projects map) first. For a GitHub App ("circleci/") destination, a project with no mapping entry is matched BY NAME against the destination org's projects (the real circleci// slug is used), so 'mapping generate' is optional; the plan prints each source → destination pair. Create the destination projects first with 'sync --apply --skip-pipelines' (it makes projects without pipeline definitions, so the GitHub App can stay installed on the source until the transfer has run). A project with no mapping entry and no match is SKIPPED, flagged in the plan, and the run exits non-zero naming it:
SKIP project "gh/acme/api": no destination project named "api" in the destination org and no mapping entry for "gh/acme/api" — create it first … TRIGGER FLAGS (REQUIRED FOR --apply): For the in-pipeline unversioned-config trigger to work, BOTH of the following flags must be enabled: 1. Org-level: allow_api_trigger_with_config (CircleCI org settings) 2. Project-level: api-trigger-with-config (per-project settings)
'secrets transfer' checks and enables both flags automatically: - In interactive mode: prompts before enabling each flag. - With --enable-trigger (non-interactive): enables both automatically. - Both flags are restored to their prior values after the transfer (defer).
WHEN TO USE:
You trust the source org's pipeline infrastructure and want the simplest, most secure migration path for context env-var values. Your destination contexts already exist or you want them auto-created. You do NOT need a local copy of the secret values. WHEN TO USE 'secrets capture' INSTEAD:
You need a local bundle for review, backup, or air-gapped flows. You are migrating SSH keys. You want to inspect values before writing them to the destination. PREREQUISITES:
Run 'export' to produce manifest.json. Store the DESTINATION org API token in a source-org context, e.g.: context name: "migration-secrets" env var: CIRCLECI_DEST_TOKEN = Pass that context name via --dest-token-context. (Optional) To transfer project env vars into a gh/ or bb/ destination, prepare a mapping.json with an entry per source project slug → destination project slug. A GitHub App destination matches projects by name instead. GitHub OAuth (gh/) and Bitbucket (bb/) source projects: CircleCI refuses to start a pipeline that checks out over SSH on a project with no CHECKOUT KEY ("the project has no SSH key"), even with inline config. In a GitHub OAuth org that also has the CircleCI GitHub App installed, each project also has GitHub App pipeline definitions, which check out with the app token and need no key; transfer prefers those automatically (the log says which definition ran). So a project needs a key only if it has NO GitHub App pipeline definition: add a deploy key under Project Settings → SSH Keys → Checkout SSH keys, or give it an App definition. OAuth triggers may stay disabled. circleci/ projects are not affected. This is checked BEFORE any context restriction is removed or trigger flag enabled: the auto-picked host is the first manifest project with a GitHub App definition, else one with a pipeline definition and a checkout key; an explicit --host-project with neither is rejected; a per-project transfer with neither is shown as SKIP, skipped on --apply, and the command exits non-zero listing it. Keys come from the manifest's checkout_keys, or are looked up live when the manifest was exported with --skip-extras. NOTE: once the GitHub App is uninstalled from the org its App definitions are gone, so project-var / SSH-key transfers then need checkout keys; contexts transferred before the uninstall do not. Contexts already transferred? Pass --skip-contexts with --include-project-vars and/or --include-ssh-keys to run only the per-project pipelines (no host project, no restriction removal, no context pipeline). Run 'secrets transfer --apply' to execute the transfer pipeline. DRY RUN (default — safe to run without --apply): Without --apply, transfer prints a plan: which contexts and variables would be transferred, whether each context would be created or updated, and (when --include-project-vars is set) per-project resolution status. No pipeline is triggered.

TRUST MODEL & SECURITY: The in-pipeline jobs need the destination API token. The CLI does NOT embed the token value in the generated config. Instead, you store the dest token in a source-org context, and the CLI embeds that context NAME. CircleCI injects the token into the job as an environment variable.
Security implication: any source-org admin who can create pipelines or attach contexts to jobs has implicit access to the dest token (the same access they have to any other sensitive context in the source org). Mitigate by: - Using a scoped API token for the destination (write to contexts only). - Rotating the dest token after the transfer is complete. - Restricting the source context holding the dest token to the minimum projects/pipelines that need it.
The dest token is referenced in the config ONLY as ${CIRCLECI_DEST_TOKEN} (or your custom --dest-token-env-var name). The literal value never appears in the generated YAML.

data.synopsis#Synopsis:
sync recreates exported data in the destination CircleCI organization.
It reads the manifest (structure + variable names), an optional secret bundle (the plaintext values captured by the in-pipeline 'secrets' step), and an optional mapping file (source->destination org/project mapping; defaults to the same names). It is idempotent: existing resources are reused by name where possible.
The destination org defaults to the SOURCE org from the manifest. To target a DIFFERENT org you MUST pass --mapping with org.to set — otherwise sync runs against your own source org (a prominent warning is printed in that case).
--mapping file schema (JSON): { "org": { "from": "gh/acme", "to": "gh/acme-new" }, "projects": { "gh/acme/web": "gh/acme-new/web" }, "github_org": { "from": "acme", "to": "acme-new" } } Only "org.to" is required to retarget the destination org. "projects" remaps individual project slugs (needed for GitHub App destinations whose slug is "circleci//"); "github_org" rewrites repo owners when repos moved to a new GitHub org.
Secrets: env-var VALUES come from the captured secret bundle (--secrets). With --apply but NO bundle, contexts/projects are created with EMPTY env-var values that you must fill in manually — run 'circleci-migrate secrets capture' first to capture the plaintext values, then pass --secrets .
Resources synced (in order): • Org settings — feature flags, OIDC claims, URL-orb allow list, config policies, OTel exporter, contacts, storage retention, budgets, release tracker, and block-unregistered-users. • Contexts — with environment variable values from the secret bundle. • Projects — OAuth projects are recreated in a paused state. App projects are created with their captured pipeline definitions and triggers (github_oauth sources are translated to github_app); an OAuth project with no captured definition gets one synthesized "build-and-test" definition, which needs --github-token (preflight fails without it). Triggers are created disabled. Re-running reconciles existing App projects: missing definitions/triggers are created, everything present reports "exists", and triggers still disabled are queued so --apply --yes enables them. A failed enable makes sync exit non-zero. • Self-hosted runner resource classes — only when --dest-runner-namespace is provided or the manifest contains runner classes.
By default sync performs a DRY RUN and writes nothing — review the plan, then re-run with --apply. Context restrictions are handled as follows: • expression — copied verbatim. • group — resolved by name to the destination group UUID (requires the group to exist in the destination; falls back to "manual" if not found). • project — remapped automatically: source project UUID → source slug → destination slug (via mapping) → destination project UUID. For a GitHub App destination, a project with no mapping entry is matched by NAME against the destination org's projects instead (no 'projects' entries needed). Requires that the destination project exists once the projects step has run; if it does not, the restriction falls back to "manual" naming the project and the fix. Re-run sync after the projects are created to resolve it.
When OAuth projects are missing in the destination, --apply creates them in a paused state (no webhook, no builds). After creation you are prompted to enable builds (follow the project, which installs the webhook and may trigger an initial build). For a GitHub App destination the prompt instead offers to enable the N triggers that were created disabled, across M projects. --yes / -y only matters together with --apply: it auto-confirms enabling builds without the interactive prompt (it has no effect in a dry run). Without a TTY, builds are not enabled unless --yes is passed.
--skip-pipelines (GitHub App destinations) creates or reuses each project and syncs its settings, env vars and other project data, but creates no pipeline definitions or triggers (reported as "skipped: --skip-pipelines"). When the manifest contains self-hosted runner resource classes, pass --dest-runner-namespace to recreate them in the destination namespace. If the flag is omitted, runner classes are flagged for manual recreation — the syncer never guesses the destination namespace.

data.synopsis#Synopsis:
generate reads an exported manifest and writes a complete set of Terraform files into --out:
versions.tf — provider version constraint (~> 0.3) providers.tf — provider block with host + org from flags contexts.tf — circleci_context + circleci_context_environment_variable resources restrictions.tf — circleci_context_restriction resources (project+expression both orgs; group OAuth-only) projects.tf — circleci_project + circleci_project_environment_variable resources webhooks.tf — circleci_webhook resources (both org types) runners.tf — circleci_runner_resource_class + circleci_runner_token resources pipelines.tf — circleci_pipeline + circleci_trigger resources (standalone ONLY) migration.auto.tfvars.json — non-secret values (context/project/webhook/pipeline/runner settings) secrets.auto.tfvars.json — env-var values (only with --secrets or --placeholders) imports.tf — Terraform 1.5+ import blocks (only with --import-existing) GAPS.md — checklist of what Terraform does not manage + CLI commands to fill gaps
The generated HCL uses for_each over variables so that regenerating after a new export changes only the tfvars, not the modules.
Apply the generated configuration:
cd ./terraform/ terraform init terraform plan terraform apply
Then run:
circleci-migrate sync --manifest manifest.json --dest-token $CIRCLECI_DEST_TOKEN --apply --skip-terraform-managed

data.synopsis#Synopsis:
validate exports BOTH the source and destination orgs (read-only), then diffs them by name/structure and prints a per-section parity report.
It reports what matched, what is missing on the destination, and what needs manual attention. Secret VALUES are never compared — they are masked by the CircleCI API and intentionally absent from the comparison.
Sections checked: • Contexts — each source context exists on destination; every env-var NAME is present; restrictions are compared by type. Contexts that only exist to run the migration — the 'secrets transfer' token context (--dest-token-context) and any --ignore-context — are left out. • Projects — each source project exists on destination (by mapped slug); every env-var NAME is present; key advanced settings match; additional SSH-key fingerprints and checkout keys are present. • Pipeline Definitions & Triggers — GitHub App destinations only: for each source project present on the destination, every pipeline definition (matched by name; config file path and provider compared) and its triggers (count, and how many are enabled). A missing definition or fewer triggers is ✗ missing; triggers still disabled are ⚠ manual. • Org Settings — feature flags, OIDC claims, URL-orb allow list, config policies, storage retention, release tracker, contacts, OTel exporters. SSO is always reported as manual (DNS verification + IdP setup required). The allow_api_trigger_with_config flag is toggled by the migration tools themselves, so a difference is shown as ℹ informational, never as missing. • Runner Classes — resource classes present in destination namespace. Requires --dest-runner-namespace; skipped with a note when absent. • Orbs — orbs and versions present in destination namespace. Requires --dest-orb-namespace; skipped with a note when absent. • CIAM — if source has CIAM data, a manual verification note is emitted (role bindings must be confirmed by email).
EXIT CODE: 0 — no missing items (✓ matched and ⚠ manual items only; manual items still require operator attention and are listed prominently). 1 — one or more items are ✗ missing on the destination.
Manual items (⚠) indicate steps that require operator action but do not by themselves cause a non-zero exit code. They are always listed in the "NEEDS ATTENTION" block regardless of the exit code.
TOKEN SOURCES (same as migrate/sync): --source-token flag or CIRCLECI_SOURCE_TOKEN env var --dest-token flag or CIRCLECI_DEST_TOKEN env var --token flag or CIRCLECI_CLI_TOKEN env var (fallback for both)
MAPPING: Pass --mapping to apply the same slug translations as 'sync'. Without a mapping, source project slugs are compared against the destination using the org-level slug derivation (gh/old/web ↔ gh/new/web when --source-org gh/old and --dest-org gh/new).

data: How it works Secrets Mapping Cutover

cutover switches builds from the source org to the destination, and you can undo it. It pauses the source, then enables the destination, and records every change in a state file so --undo can put it all back.
Without it, you would enable the destination with sync --yes and leave both orgs building. Use cutover whenever the source is still live.
flowchart LR P[1. pause source] --> M[2. move GitHub App - point of no return] M --> S[3. sync definitions and triggers] S --> E[4. enable destination] P -. undo .-> U[cutover --undo] E -. undo .-> UStep 2 applies only to OAuth to GitHub App. After the GitHub App leaves the source org, --undo cannot bring back the source's App triggers.
data.after-the-cutover#After the cutover: Do not build in both orgs. You would pay twice. Repoint what references the old org: service catalogs, badges, Slack and notification integrations, required status checks, and scripts with hard-coded project or context IDs. Rotate the secrets that moved and delete the migration-secrets context. Delete cutover-state.json once you are sure you will not undo. When the destination is healthy, decommission the source: unfollow its projects, archive its contexts, and tell your team and outside contributors.
data.keep-these-files-safe#Keep these files s: cutover-state.json: without it --undo has nothing to restore from. webhook-secrets.json: holds the new webhook signing secrets and URLs, mode 0600, never printed. It is merged on re-runs, not overwritten. Delete both once the cutover is confirmed and every sender and receiver has its new value.
data.no-live-source#No live source: If nothing is building in the source, skip cutover and enable the destination directly with sync --apply --yes. On a re-run, add --enable-existing-triggers to enable triggers that already exist and are still disabled.
data.order-for-app-to-app#Order for App to Ap:
The destination projects, definitions and triggers already exist after sync --apply, so one step does the switch:
circleci-migrate cutover --manifest manifest.json --mapping mapping.json --pause-source --enable-dest circleci-migrate cutover --manifest manifest.json --mapping mapping.json --pause-source --enable-dest --apply Check: every item prints set or exists, and the exit code is 0.
data.order-for-oauth-to-github-app#Order for:
The order is fixed. Secrets transfer needs a source that can still build, and the source's App triggers vanish when the App is uninstalled. The full steps are in the runbook.
Freeze merges in the source repos. sync --skip-pipelines --apply to create the destination projects. secrets transfer ... --apply while the source can still build. cutover --pause-source --apply. Move the GitHub App: uninstall it from the source org, install it from the destination org. sync --apply --webhook-secrets-out webhook-secrets.json to add definitions and triggers. Answer N at the enable prompt. cutover --enable-dest --apply. validate, then a smoke push. Caution Step 5 is the point of no return. Uninstalling the GitHub App deletes the source org's App pipelines and triggers. The export is the only record. Pause the source first.
data.order-for-oauth-to-oauth#Order for OAuth:
--enable-dest acts on triggers, so it does nothing for an OAuth destination. An OAuth destination goes live when its projects are followed, which is the enable-builds prompt of sync --apply. Once the destination is validated, pause the source:
circleci-migrate cutover --manifest manifest.json --pause-source --apply Add --pause-org to pause the whole source org.
data.the-flags#The flags:
cutover is a dry run until you add --apply. Each item prints with its outcome, and the command exits non-zero if any item fails. Re-running is safe.
Flag What it does --pause-source On each source OAuth project, sets drop-all-build-requests=true (the old value is recorded) and disables the source triggers that are enabled and are not github_oauth triggers. Never unfollows a project. --pause-org Also sets drop-all-build-requests on the whole source org. Use with --pause-source. --enable-dest Enables each destination trigger whose source trigger was enabled. A trigger disabled in the source stays disabled. --undo Restores everything in the state file: source flags, source triggers, and destination triggers it enabled. --state State file path. Default cutover-state.json, mode 0600. --manifest, --mapping Needed for pause and enable. With --undo they only check that the state file matches your orgs. --enable-dest matches triggers by name, then by their fields. An ambiguous match, and a project the manifest shows as paused or not followed, is reported manual and left disabled. Enable that trigger by hand in Project Settings > Triggers. Run sync --apply first so the destination triggers exist.
If a pause fails in the same run, nothing is enabled.
data.undo#Undo:
circleci-migrate cutover --undo --apply Check: the source flags and triggers are back, and the destination triggers it enabled are disabled again.
--undo needs only the state file. It is safe to repeat and fails if the file is missing or belongs to another org. A state record is kept when a change fails in a way that may have applied it (a timeout or a 5xx).
Can undo Cannot undo Source drop-all-build-requests flags. Moving the GitHub App. A GitHub org connects to one CircleCI org at a time, so uninstall it from the new org and reinstall it on the old one yourself. Source triggers that cutover disabled, while the App is still installed. Source App triggers, once the App has been uninstalled. Only the flag comes back. Destination triggers that cutover enabled. Anything you changed outside cutover.

data:
A migration is five steps: export the source, move the secrets, sync the structure, cut over, validate. Each step is a circleci-migrate command, and every command that writes is a dry run until you add --apply.
flowchart LR E[export] --> M[(manifest.json)] M --> S[secrets transfer] M --> Y[sync] S --> Y Y --> C[cutover] C --> V[validate] C -. undo .-> YThe order of the middle steps changes with the migration type. Follow the runbook for yours: OAuth to GitHub App, OAuth to OAuth or App to App.
data.checks-before-you-start#Checks before yo:
Run doctor first. It is read-only and checks tokens, org reachability, the allow_api_trigger_with_config setting and the GitHub token.
circleci-migrate doctor --source-org "$SOURCE_ORG" --dest-org "$DEST_ORG" Check: it exits 0. Exit 1 means a hard failure, such as a missing token or an unreachable org. export, sync and migrate run the same checks on startup; --skip-preflight turns them off.
data.dry-run-first#Dry run first:
sync, secrets transfer, cutover and migrate change nothing until you pass --apply. A dry run prints each action as one of these:
Status Meaning created (would create) --apply will create it. set (would set) --apply will write the value. exists Already there; reused. Re-runs are safe. manual The API cannot do it. The report says what to do by hand. error A problem. Fix it before you apply. New projects are created paused: no builds run in the destination until you enable them.
data.orbs-and-runner-classes#Orbs and runner:
Orb namespaces and runner resource classes belong to one org, so they need extra steps.
Different destination namespace. sync --dest-orb-namespace republishes every stable version. A notice lists each old/orb to new/orb reference to rewrite in your configs. Same namespace name. An orb namespace cannot exist in two orgs. Ask CircleCI support to move it to the destination org. The orbs move with it and configs need no change. Runner classes. --runner-namespace on export and --dest-runner-namespace on sync recreate class definitions only. Instances and tokens do not move. After a same-name namespace move, classes stay attributed to the source org. Delete the source copies, re-run sync, create new tokens and re-register agents.
data.the-all-in-one-command#The all-in-one co:
migrate runs export, sync and validate in one go. With no flags on a terminal it starts a guided walkthrough, then shows a dry run and asks before it applies.
circleci-migrate migrate --source-org "$SOURCE_ORG" --dest-org "$DEST_ORG" \ --transfer-secrets --dest-token-context migration-secrets --include-project-vars The walkthrough asks which components to migrate (contexts, projects, org settings, extras, orbs, runners) and how to move secrets. Check: it prints a summary with counts and a "Needs attention" list. Add --apply to write.
Use the step-by-step commands for production moves, especially OAuth to GitHub App. migrate cannot do the pause and App-move steps in the right order.
data.the-circleci-cli-plugin#The circleci CLI: circleci run migrate runs circleci-migrate and passes CIRCLE_TOKEN and CIRCLE_URL for you. Bare circleci migrate is not supported.
data.the-five-steps#The five steps: Step Command What it does Export export Reads the source org and writes manifest.json and migration-report.md. Read-only. Secrets secrets transfer Moves secret values from source to destination without writing them to disk. See Secrets. Sync sync Replays the manifest into the destination org. Dry run unless --apply. Cutover cutover Pauses source builds and enables destination builds, reversibly. See Cutover. Validate validate Compares source and destination and exits 1 if anything is missing. mapping.json tells sync where the destination is. See Mapping.
data.the-manifest#The manifest:
manifest.json is a snapshot of the source org: structure and names, never secret values. It is safe to read, diff and store.
The CircleCI API never returns a secret value, so the manifest lists variable names only. migration-report.md sits next to it. It lists everything captured and the manual follow-ups for your org. Read it before you sync.
Re-export whenever the source changes. Every later command reads the manifest, not the live source.
data.tokens-and-slugs#Tokens and slugs:
Use a personal API token for each side, from User Settings > Personal API Tokens. The token's user must be an organization admin of the org it acts on.
Variable Used for CIRCLECI_SOURCE_TOKEN Reading the source org. CIRCLECI_DEST_TOKEN Writing the destination org. CIRCLECI_CLI_TOKEN or CIRCLE_TOKEN Fallback for both sides. GITHUB_TOKEN Repo read. Needed for OAuth to App and for repos moving to a new GitHub org. The org slug decides which APIs the tool uses.
Org type Slug Notes GitHub OAuth gh/ Projects are followed to install webhooks. Bitbucket OAuth bb/ Same as GitHub OAuth. GitHub App, GitLab or standalone circleci/ Projects use pipeline definitions and triggers. Standalone orgs also carry roles and groups. Note One GitHub org can have both an OAuth record (gh/acme) and an App record (circleci/). They are separate orgs. Migrate each one on its own.
For CircleCI Server, pass --host https://circleci.example.com (or set CIRCLECI_CLI_HOST). The default is https://circleci.com.
data.what-sync-does#What sync does: Order. Contexts come before projects. A project-type context restriction needs its destination project, so the first run can report it manual. Re-run sync --apply to resolve it. Re-runs. A re-run creates only what is missing and reports the rest exists. A trigger you disabled on purpose is not re-enabled unless you pass --enable-existing-triggers. Enabling builds. After creating projects, sync asks whether to enable builds. --yes answers for you. Do not use --yes while the source is still building, or both orgs build. Use cutover. Danger flags. drop_all_build_requests and require_context_group_restriction are skipped by default because they can freeze a new org. Add --include-danger-flags once the destination is validated. Webhook secrets. CircleCI never returns signing secrets. --webhook-secrets-out webhook-secrets.json writes new ones (mode 0600, never printed). Hand each sender and receiver its new value. Project API tokens. Recreated only with --create-project-tokens, and each one is a new value. Scoping. --skip-org-settings, --skip-contexts, --skip-projects, --skip-pipelines, --skip-extras, --skip-runner, --skip-ciam and --skip-orb leave a section alone.

data:
mapping.json tells the CLI where the destination is. You need it whenever the destination org differs from the source, and the only line that is always required is org.to.
Without it, sync targets the source org named in the manifest and prints a warning. That is correct only when you re-apply into the same org.
data.generate-it#Generate it:
Generate the file from the manifest. For an OAuth destination it fills in every project. For a GitHub App destination, write the org line first, run sync --apply --skip-pipelines to create the projects, then generate.
circleci-migrate mapping generate --manifest manifest.json --dest-org "$DEST_ORG" --output mapping.json Check: mapping.json has org.from set to your source and org.to set to the destination.
mapping generate writes only org and projects. Add github_org back by hand if you use it.
data.partial-repo-moves#Partial repo moves:
When only some repos changed GitHub org, use projects entries for those repos. Use github_org when every repo moved. Resolving the new repo IDs needs a GitHub token with repo read:
export GITHUB_TOKEN="" circleci-migrate sync --manifest manifest.json --mapping mapping.json --apply Check: no project shows manual for a wrong external_id.
data.project-entries-are-optional#Project ent:
A GitHub App project slug is circleci//, and the project ID exists only after the project does. You cannot write these entries up front.
You do not have to. For a source project with no entry, project-type context restrictions and secrets transfer --include-project-vars match the destination project by name. An entry always wins over a name match. Add entries only to review a match or override it.
data.schema#Schema:
{ "org": { "from": "gh/acme", "to": "circleci/22222222-2222-2222-2222-222222222222" }, "projects": { "gh/acme/web": "circleci/22222222-2222-2222-2222-222222222222/3f1c0b52-7d0e-4a57-9a53-0a6d4f1e9b10" }, "github_org": { "from": "acme", "to": "acme-new" } } All three keys are optional except org.to.
Key Meaning org Source and destination org slugs. to retargets the destination. from should match the manifest. projects Source project slug to destination project slug. Optional for most moves. github_org Rewrites the GitHub owner of every repo. Overrides --dest-github-org. Needs --github-token. An entry in projects whose key has no / maps a context name to a destination context name. This applies to secrets transfer --mapping.
data.see-also#See also: How it works Troubleshooting sync flags
data.when-you-need-it#When you need it: Situation What to put in mapping.json Destination org name differs from the source org with from and to. Slug type changes, such as gh/acme to circleci/ org.to set to the destination slug. sync finds or creates App projects by name. Repos moved to a new GitHub org github_org with from and to, or per-project projects entries. Same org, same names No mapping file. migrate also accepts --mapping. For a straight same-name move you can pass --dest-org to migrate instead.

data:
Use secrets transfer to move secret values. It sends them from the source org to the destination org without writing them to disk. Use secrets capture only when you need a local, reviewable bundle.
CircleCI never returns a secret value through its API. The only place a value can be read is inside a running pipeline of the org that owns it, so both methods run a short-lived pipeline in your source org.
flowchart LR CLI[circleci-migrate] -->|inline pipeline| SRC[Source org job] SRC -->|PUT over TLS| DST[Destination org API] TOK[(migration-secrets context)] -.->|CIRCLECI_DEST_TOKEN| SRC
data.after-the-move#After the move: Rotate every value that moved. Treat each as exposed once it left the source. Delete the migration-secrets context from the source org, or rotate its token. Delete secrets.json and any decrypted copies, if you used capture. Spot-check the destination: variable names and counts match. Values stay masked, and validate compares names, not values.
data.capture-the-local-bundle#Capture: the lo:
secrets capture runs the same kind of pipeline but writes the values to an encrypted artifact, downloads it and saves a local secrets.json. sync --secrets secrets.json then writes the values as it creates each resource.
circleci-migrate secrets capture --manifest manifest.json \ --encrypt --generate-key --artifact-retention-days 1 --enable-trigger \ --output secrets.json Check: secrets.json exists with mode 0600. Capture before sync.
Flag Use --encrypt On by default. Encrypts the artifact with age so plaintext never sits in CircleCI. --generate-key Creates a fresh age keypair. Or pass --ssh-public-key and --ssh-private-key. --artifact-retention-days 1 Shortens how long the artifact stays in CircleCI. --storage artifact (default), s3 or both. S3 needs --s3-bucket and optionally --s3-prefix. --context, --project Limit what is captured. --ssh-keys=false Skip additional SSH keys, which are captured by default. --remove-restrictions Lift context restrictions for the run. By default restricted contexts are skipped. --yes Allow an unattended capture of everything. Without it, a non-interactive run with no --context or --project stops. Restricted contexts skipped at capture can still get their variable names: sync --missing-secrets placeholder creates each name with a placeholder value to fill in later.
secrets decrypt decrypts a bundle you downloaded yourself. For many contexts, the awesomecicd/circleci-org-migration orb runs one extract_context job per context, then a merge job. Use one context per job so same-named variables cannot overwrite each other.
Warning Do not mix methods for the same resources. A bundle contains plaintext values. Keep it out of git, and delete it after the sync.
data.key-flags#Key flags: Flag Use --dest-org-id Destination org UUID (Organization Settings > Overview). A slug is rejected. --dest-org also works and is resolved for you. --dest-token-context Name of the source-org context holding the destination token. --include-project-vars Also move project env vars. Needs the destination project to exist. --include-ssh-keys Also move additional project SSH keys. --remove-restrictions Lift project and expression restrictions on contexts for the run, then restore them. Group restrictions are never touched. --enable-trigger Turn on allow_api_trigger_with_config for the run and restore it afterwards. --skip-contexts Run only the per-project pipelines, for contexts already moved. --host-project Source project that runs the context pipeline. Defaults to a suitable one.
data.rules-that-decide-the-order#Rules that d: Destination projects must exist before you move project vars or SSH keys. Contexts are created for you. For a GitHub App destination, create the projects first with sync --apply --skip-pipelines. Projects are matched by name. For a GitHub App destination a source project with no projects entry in mapping.json is matched to the destination project of the same name. An entry always wins. A project that matches neither is shown as SKIP, and the run exits non-zero. The source must still be able to build. Run the transfer before cutover --pause-source. It fails fast and names any paused project. gh/ and bb/ source projects need a way to check out. CircleCI will not start a pipeline on them without a GitHub App pipeline definition or a checkout key. The CLI prefers an App definition and checks this before it changes anything. Move secrets before the GitHub App leaves the source org. After the uninstall the App definitions are gone, and every project then needs a checkout key. Contexts with project or expression restrictions block the pipeline unless you pass --remove-restrictions. If a restore fails, the CLI prints the exact restriction to re-add.
data.transfer-the-recommended-method#Transfer:
The CLI submits one inline pipeline to the source org. Inside it, CircleCI injects the real values and the job writes each one straight to the destination. No value reaches your laptop, an artifact or storage.
The job needs a destination API token. Put it in a context in the source org and pass the context's name. The generated config references ${CIRCLECI_DEST_TOKEN} and never contains the token.
# 1. In the SOURCE org, create a context named migration-secrets # holding CIRCLECI_DEST_TOKEN (a destination org-admin token). # 2. Dry run: prints the plan, triggers nothing. circleci-migrate secrets transfer --manifest manifest.json --mapping mapping.json \ --dest-org-id "$DEST_ORG_ID" --dest-token-context migration-secrets \ --include-project-vars --include-ssh-keys --remove-restrictions # 3. Apply. circleci-migrate secrets transfer --manifest manifest.json --mapping mapping.json \ --dest-org-id "$DEST_ORG_ID" --dest-token-context migration-secrets \ --include-project-vars --include-ssh-keys --remove-restrictions --enable-trigger --apply Check: the plan lists each context and project with [create] or [update] and no SKIP lines. After --apply, the destination shows the same variable names.
Note Anyone who can create pipelines in the source org can read the token context. Use a token with the least access that works, and rotate it when the transfer is done.
data.what-does-not-move#What does not move: Item Why What to do Checkout and deploy key private keys No API returns them. Add a deploy key in the destination. A GitHub App destination needs none. Webhook signing secrets The source values are unreadable. sync --webhook-secrets-out generates new ones. Project API token values Shown once, at creation. sync --create-project-tokens mints new values. Repoint consumers. Restricted-context values The pipeline cannot read them without --remove-restrictions. Re-run with the flag, or fill in by hand.

data: Architecture API usage Testing Decision records: The significant architecture decisions, one short page each. 1. Thin REST clients instead of a third-party SDK 2. Inline (unversioned) pipeline config for secret-value capture 3. Create projects paused, then enable them explicitly 4. Two-host client design (app.circleci.com vs circleci.com) Docs site: How the site is built and published, and how to move it to CircleCI-Labs.

data.consequences#Consequences: Full control over every request (escaped paths, methods, headers, page sizes) and clear visibility into which API surface each call hits. We can mix v2, v1.1, v3, and private endpoints freely as the migration needs dictate, without waiting on an SDK to expose them. We carry the maintenance cost of the HTTP layer and must track API changes ourselves; this is mitigated by wire-level httptest tests that assert request details. Aligns with the official CLI's style, easing a potential future merge.
data.context#Context:
The CLI talks to several CircleCI API surfaces (v2, v1.1, v3, the private CIAM BFF, and a private project-list endpoint). It is modeled structurally on CircleCI-Public/circleci-cli so that it could one day merge into the official CLI. We needed to decide whether to depend on a generated or third-party Go SDK or to own the HTTP layer directly.
No single SDK covers all of the surfaces we use — in particular the private CIAM/groups endpoints and the private project-list endpoint. A heavy SDK dependency would also complicate an eventual merge into the official CLI and obscure exactly which endpoints and JSON shapes we depend on.
data.decision#Decision: Own thin REST clients under api/ (org, context, project, plus a shared rest client). No third-party CircleCI SDK. Each client method is small and documents the exact endpoint, method, and request/response JSON shape it uses.

/circleci-org-migration-cli/docs/contrib.title: 1. Thin REST clients instead of a third-party SDK

data.consequences#Consequences: Secret values can be captured with no committed configuration in the customer's repositories — nothing is left behind in source control. Requires the ability to toggle api-trigger-with-config; the tool restores the original value to avoid leaving the org in a changed state. The capture pipeline must run on a project; contexts can be captured via any project, while project env-vars run under their own project. Values transit a pipeline artifact; this is handled with storage-access controls and (optionally) encryption rather than persisting plaintext longer than necessary.
data.context#Context:
Context and project environment-variable values are masked by the CircleCI API on read — only the variable names are returned. Migrating an org faithfully requires transferring the actual secret values, so we needed a way to obtain them without asking the operator to re-enter every secret by hand, and without committing any helper configuration into the source org's repositories.
A pipeline running inside the source org can read the values it has access to. The question was how to run such a pipeline without modifying the customer's committed .circleci/config.yml.
data.decision#Decision:
secrets capture runs an inline (unversioned) pipeline config: it temporarily enables api-trigger-with-config (at org and project scope), triggers a pipeline via POST .../pipeline/run with an inline config.content that dumps the exported variable names and attached contexts to an artifact, polls for completion, downloads the artifact, parses the values, and aggregates them client-side. The api-trigger-with-config setting is restored to its prior state afterward.
An orb (extract_context / extract_project jobs) provides the same capability as an in-pipeline alternative for teams that prefer to drive it from their own config.

/circleci-org-migration-cli/docs/contrib.title: 2. Inline (unversioned) pipeline config for secret-value capture

data.consequences#Consequences: Migration can create the full destination project structure without triggering unintended builds, supporting a controlled cutover. The operator gets a clear, auditable enable step and can verify the migrated setup before going live. Slightly more API work (create-then-PATCH) versus creating already-enabled triggers, in exchange for safety during cutover.
data.context#Context: When syncing to a GitHub App destination org, project creation involves a chain: create the project, create its pipeline-definitions, then create triggers. Once triggers are live, the destination project can start building on incoming events. During a migration the operator may not be ready for the destination org to react to webhooks immediately — premature builds could fire before the cutover is intended, or before the operator has verified the migrated configuration.
data.decision#Decision: For GitHub App destinations, create each trigger disabled (paused) and enable it as a distinct, explicit step: PATCH .../triggers {disabled:false}. Enabling builds is gated behind an interactive confirmation prompt (or --yes for non-interactive runs). This makes "the destination starts building" a deliberate operator action rather than a side effect of project creation.

/circleci-org-migration-cli/docs/contrib.title: 3. Create projects paused, then enable them explicitly

data.consequences#Consequences: Calls land on the host that actually serves them; the v1.1-PUT-on-circleci.com path for feature flags is encoded once and reused, avoiding the 404 trap. The code makes the host/version split visible at the call site, which helps future maintainers reason about CircleCI's heterogeneous API surface. Adding a new capability requires knowing (and recording) which host/version serves it; this is a deliberate, low cost given the alternative of silent wrong-host failures.
data.context#Context:
Different CircleCI capabilities live behind different hosts and API versions, and they are not interchangeable:
Most v2 work and the private project-list endpoint use the standard REST host. The private CIAM BFF (org groups, SSO) lives on app.circleci.com. Some org/project settings are only writable via v1.1 on circleci.com — notably feature-flag writes, which are a PUT .../api/v1.1/.../settings. The equivalent POST against app.circleci.com returns 404 (verified live). Treating these as one base URL led to wrong-host calls failing.
data.decision#Decision: Model the destinations explicitly so each call is routed to the correct host and API version. The REST client layer distinguishes the standard host from the app.circleci.com host, and v1.1 feature-flag writes are sent as PUT to circleci.com rather than to app.circleci.com. Each client method documents which host/version it targets.
